statement: Prove that the closed interval [a,b] is compact in the standard topology on R.
solution: Let U be an open cover of [a,b] and S={x∈[a,b] : [a,x] is covered by finitely many members of U}. S contains a and is bounded above by b; let c=sup S. Some U0∈U contains c, with (c-ε,c+ε)⊆U0. Pick x∈S with x>c-ε (possible as c=sup S); then [a,x] is finitely covered, and adjoining U0 finitely covers [a,c+ε)∩[a,b]. So c∈S and, were c<b, some point beyond c would also lie in S — contradiction. Hence c=b∈S and [a,b] is finitely covered.

statement: Prove that every finite topological space is compact.
solution: A topology on a finite set has only finitely many open sets, so any open cover is already a finite collection of open sets; a finite subcover exists trivially (the cover itself).

statement: State the tube lemma and use it to prove that the product of two compact spaces is compact.
solution: Tube lemma: if Y is compact and N is open in X×Y containing the slice {x0}×Y, then some tube W×Y⊆N with W a nbhd of x0. Proof of product compactness: given an open cover of X×Y, each slice {x}×Y is compact so finitely covered; the union of those finitely many sets contains a tube W_x×Y (tube lemma). The W_x cover compact X; take a finite subcover; the corresponding finitely many tubes, each finitely covered, finitely cover X×Y.

statement: Prove that two disjoint compact subsets of a Hausdorff space can be separated by disjoint open sets.
solution: First, a point and a disjoint compact set can be separated (compact-Hausdorff regularity): for p∉K, use Hausdorff to get disjoint opens around p and each y∈K, take a finite subcover of K, intersect the p-neighborhoods. Now for disjoint compact A,B: for each a∈A separate a from B by disjoint opens U_a∋a, V_a⊇B; the U_a cover A, take finite subcover U_{a1..an}, let U=∪U_{ai}, V=∩V_{ai}. Then U⊇A, V⊇B are disjoint opens.

statement: Prove that a compact subset of R attains a maximum and a minimum.
solution: A compact subset K of R is closed and bounded. Boundedness gives finite sup and inf; closedness gives sup K, inf K ∈ K (a point outside a closed set has a neighborhood missing K, impossible for the sup/inf). So the max and min are attained.

statement: Prove the finite intersection property characterization: X is compact if and only if every family of closed sets with the finite intersection property has nonempty intersection.
solution: Take complements. An open cover {U_i} with no finite subcover corresponds to closed sets {X\U_i} such that no finite subfamily covers, i.e. every finite intersection of the X\U_i is nonempty (FIP), yet the total intersection ∩(X\U_i)=X\∪U_i is empty exactly when {U_i} covers. So 'every open cover has a finite subcover' is equivalent to 'every closed family with FIP has nonempty intersection.'

statement: Prove that a nested sequence of nonempty compact closed sets C_1 ⊇ C_2 ⊇ ... has nonempty intersection.
solution: The C_n have the finite intersection property: any finite subfamily's intersection is the smallest C_n in it, which is nonempty. By the FIP characterization of compactness (k06), applied within the compact space C_1, the total intersection ∩C_n is nonempty.

statement: Prove that in a metric space, compactness implies sequential compactness.
solution: Let (x_n) be a sequence in compact metric X. If it had no convergent subsequence, every point would have a neighborhood containing x_n for only finitely many n; these neighborhoods cover X, and a finite subcover would contain only finitely many terms — impossible for an infinite sequence. So some subsequence converges.

statement: Prove that a continuous function from a compact metric space to a metric space is uniformly continuous.
solution: Given ε>0, for each x pick δ_x with f(B(x,δ_x))⊆B(f(x),ε/2). The balls B(x,δ_x/2) cover X; take a Lebesgue number λ>0 (exists by compactness). If d(a,b)<λ then a,b lie in some B(x,δ_x), so d(f(a),f(b))<ε. Hence f is uniformly continuous.

statement: State and prove the Lebesgue number lemma for a compact metric space.
solution: Claim: for any open cover of a compact metric space X there is λ>0 such that every set of diameter <λ lies in some cover member. Proof: for each x, some ball B(x,ε_x) lies in a cover member; the balls B(x,ε_x/2) cover X, take a finite subcover with centers x_1..x_n; let λ=min ε_{x_i}/2. Any set S of diameter <λ meets some B(x_i,ε_{x_i}/2), so S⊆B(x_i,ε_{x_i})⊆ a cover member.

statement: Prove that a compact metric space is complete.
solution: Let (x_n) be Cauchy in compact metric X. By sequential compactness (k08) some subsequence converges to a point p. A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges to the same limit p. Hence every Cauchy sequence converges and X is complete.

statement: Prove that a compact subspace of a metric space is bounded and closed.
solution: Compact ⇒ closed requires Hausdorff, and metric spaces are Hausdorff, so K is closed. For bounded: fix x0; the balls B(x0,n), n∈N, cover K; a finite subcover gives K⊆B(x0,N), so K is bounded.

statement: Prove that a closed subspace of a compact Hausdorff space is compact Hausdorff.
solution: A closed subset of a compact space is compact (add the complement to any open cover, extract a finite subcover, discard the complement). Hausdorffness is hereditary: distinct points of the subspace are separated by the intersections of ambient separating opens with the subspace.

statement: Prove the Heine-Borel theorem: a subset of R^n is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
solution: (⇒) Compact subsets of the Hausdorff space R^n are closed, and bounded by k12. (⇐) A closed bounded set lies in some box [-M,M]^n, which is compact as a finite product of compact intervals [a,b] (k01, k03). A closed subset of a compact set is compact, so the set is compact.

statement: Prove that if X is compact and f: X → R is continuous, then f is bounded.
solution: f(X) is compact in R (continuous image of compact), hence bounded (k12). So f is bounded on X.

statement: Prove that a finite union of compact subspaces is compact.
solution: Let K=K_1∪...∪K_n with each K_i compact. Given an open cover of K, it covers each K_i; take a finite subcover of each and union these n finite collections to get a finite subcover of K.

statement: Prove that the image of a compact space under a continuous map is compact.
solution: Let f:X→Y continuous, X compact. Given an open cover {V_i} of f(X), the sets f^{-1}(V_i) form an open cover of X; extract a finite subcover f^{-1}(V_{i1}),...,f^{-1}(V_{ik}). Then V_{i1},...,V_{ik} cover f(X). Hence f(X) is compact.

statement: Prove that the one-point compactification of a locally compact Hausdorff space is compact.
solution: Let X*=X∪{∞} with open sets = opens of X together with sets {∞}∪(X\C) for C⊆X compact. Given an open cover of X*, some member contains ∞ and thus has the form {∞}∪(X\C) with C compact. The remaining cover members cover C; take a finite subcover of C and add the ∞-set to cover all of X*. Hence X* is compact.
